5 Portable Power Stations With A Built-In 30-Amp RV Outlet (TT-30) Skip to content 
 There’s a moment that sells a power station to an RVer: your rig’s 30-amp shore cord, the thick cord you plug into the power post at a campsite, goes straight into a battery instead. No adapters, and the whole rig wakes up. No generator running, no quiet hours to worry about.
 That only works if the station has a TT-30 outlet . It’s the same round, three-prong 30-amp, 120-volt socket you plug into at a campground’s power post, the pedestal (TT stands for travel trailer). Without one, you end up stacking dogbone adapters (short adapter cords) on a 15- or 20-amp household outlet and living with whatever that one outlet can give.
 Of the five stations here, the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is the one we’d pick. Its TT-30 is rated for the full 30 amps, its inverter (the part that turns battery power into household power) can deliver the 3,600 watts that implies, and it rolls on wheels. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 has the most power, and the BLUETTI Elite 300 is the lightest.

 Can a power station really run your RV through the TT-30? 
 Yes, for most of the rig, and not for as long as you’d hope. Plug your shore cord into the station, and the RV treats it like a campground pedestal: outlets, lights, fans, the furnace blower and the fridge on electric all work.
 What changes is the supply. A 30-amp pedestal gives you 3,600 watts (120 volts times 30 amps) for as long as you’re parked. A station gives you its inverter’s rated watts until the battery runs out, and how long that takes depends on its capacity in watt-hours (Wh). A 3,000 Wh battery runs a 1,000-watt load for about three hours, a bit less once the inverter takes its share. A kWh is 1,000 Wh.
 Two numbers decide what your RV gets. One is the amp rating on the TT-30 outlet. The other is the station’s continuous AC output, which is shared by every outlet on it. The smaller of the two is your ceiling. Four of the five stations below are rated for the full 30 amps on the TT-30 and have an inverter big enough to back it up. The BLUETTI Elite 300 has the outlet, but the whole station tops out at 2,400 watts, so the RV gets about 20 amps through it.
 The air conditioner is where it falls apart. Dometic lists its FreshJet 5 13.5K rooftop air conditioner at 12.8 to 19.7 amps while cooling, at 115 volts. That’s roughly 1,500 to 2,300 watts. On a 3,000 Wh station, that’s somewhere between an hour and 20 minutes and two hours, before inverter losses, and the compressor’s kick at startup is bigger still.
 These stations are great for a fridge, lights, fans, laptops and the coffee maker. They don’t replace a pedestal on a 95-degree afternoon.
 Watch the converter. Your RV’s converter sees the station as shore power and starts charging the house batteries. A 55-amp converter charging at about 14 volts puts out close to 800 watts, and every one of them comes out of the station. If the house batteries are already full, or you’d rather keep the station’s charge for the evening, switch the converter off at its breaker. This is something we do daily in our RV.

 My take
 Jackery rates the TT-30 outlet at 30 amps and 3,600 watts, with a 3,600-watt inverter behind it and a 7,200-watt surge (a short burst for motors that pull extra power as they start). So your RV gets everything a 30-amp pedestal would give it, for as long as the 3,584 Wh lasts. Of the four stations here that deliver the full 30 amps, this one carries the most battery for its weight: 3,584 Wh at 77 pounds, where the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus carries 3,072 Wh at 74 and the DELTA Pro 3 needs 114 pounds for its 4,096 Wh. That’s why it’s our pick.
 Like all five here, it uses LiFePO4 cells (lithium iron phosphate, also written LFP), a battery type built for thousands of charges. Jackery rates it for 6,000 cycles to 70%: about 6,000 full charges before it holds 70% of what it did new.
 It grows with Jackery’s add-on batteries, up to 21 kWh, it rolls on wheels, and it has a quiet mode Jackery puts at 30 dB, about the level of a whisper. We’ve reviewed several Jackery stations, like the Explorer 2000 Pro .
 Fair warning: solar input tops out at 1,000 watts. Even in perfect sun that’s more than three and a half hours to refill it, and real panels rarely make their full rating. At about 77 pounds, the wheels earn their place.

 The extra 400 watts over our pick never reach your RV. EcoFlow rates the TT-30 at 30 amps, so 3,600 watts is still the ceiling through the shore cord. The 4,000 watts is what all the outlets share, and one of those is a 240-volt L14-30, the kind a home backup setup plugs into. That makes it as much a home backup battery as an RV one.
 The battery is LFP, rated by EcoFlow for 4,000 cycles to 80%, and it takes up to 2,600 watts of solar. It also has a 30-amp Anderson port, the chunky square plug that high-current 12-volt gear often uses. We’ve reviewed a few EcoFlow stations over the years, including the DELTA 2 and the DELTA Max .
 It has wheels, and it needs them: EcoFlow lists it at 113.54 pounds. Its page also showed “Limited Stock” when we checked in October 2026. If the RV is all you’re powering, the extra output mostly sits unused.

 The Elite 300 carries more battery for its weight than anything else here: 3,014 Wh at about 58 pounds, which makes it the lightest of the five by more than 15 pounds.
 The catch is the outlet. The TT-30 is there, but BLUETTI gives it no rating of its own, and the whole AC side is limited to 2,400 watts. That works out to about 20 amps at 120 volts, two-thirds of what the plug shape suggests. Everyday loads won’t notice. A microwave and a coffee maker running at the same time is where you’ll find the edge.
 It can’t take add-on batteries, so 3,014 Wh is what you get. Solar input is up to 1,200 watts, at 12 to 60 volts. We’ve tested several BLUETTI stations, like the AC70 and the EB55 .

 The Apex 300 starts smaller than the others here, at 2,765 Wh, but takes up to six of BLUETTI’s B300K add-on batteries, so it’s built to be the first piece of a bigger setup. BLUETTI rates its TT-30 at 120 volts and 30 amps, and the 3,840-watt inverter covers that with a little room to spare.
 Its 12-volt Anderson port is rated 50 amps (the EcoFlows and the Elite 300 stop at 30), and solar goes in through two inputs of 1,200 watts each.
 The downside is weight. At 84 pounds it’s heavy for 2,765 Wh on its own, and without add-on batteries the Jackery holds more for less weight. On noise BLUETTI gives one figure, a maximum of 50 dB, so we can’t say how it compares with the others on a quiet night at camp.

 What about the stations on older TT-30 lists? 
 You’ll still see the original EcoFlow DELTA Pro, the BLUETTI AC200MAX, the Anker SOLIX F2000 and the Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus on many TT-30 lists. When we checked the makers’ US sites in October 2026, BLUETTI showed the AC200MAX as sold out, Anker’s F2000 page redirected to the newer C2000 Gen 2, and Jackery sold the 2000 Plus only refurbished. EcoFlow’s spec page for the original DELTA Pro doesn’t list a TT-30 outlet, so we left it out. EcoFlow’s documented 30-amp RV outlets are on the DELTA Pro 3 and the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus.
 If you do find a refurbished Explorer 2000 Plus, know that Jackery rates its 30-amp-style outlet at 25 amps.
 The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 where the F2000 page now sends you, has a TT-30 too, but Anker rates it at 20 amps, about the same ceiling the Elite 300 works under. At 41.7 pounds it’s far easier to move, so if 20 amps covers what you run, it’s worth a look.
 Who should skip the TT-30 altogether? 
 If you mostly camp with hookups, the pedestal already does this job, and a station with a TT-30 is a heavy box to haul around for the odd night without one. The same goes if you expect to run the air conditioner off a battery all afternoon: the math above doesn’t work out on any of these five.
 If you only need to charge phones and run lights, a much smaller station covers that, and our roundup has the ones we’ve tested.
 Not sure whether your rig is 30 or 50 amp? Here’s how 30-amp and 50-amp RVs differ . A 50-amp rig can use a TT-30 station through a 50-to-30 dogbone adapter, but then you’re working with 30 amps.
 If you go the generator route instead, we’ve covered connecting a generator to a 30 or 50-amp RV . Whichever power source you use, a surge protector belongs in the chain, and a good 30-amp extension cord rounds out the kit.
 Which one should you buy? 
 The short version: a 30-amp rig that should work exactly as it does on a pedestal gets the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus . A battery that has to back up the house between trips gets the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 . If you’ll be lifting it in and out of a truck bed, the BLUETTI Elite 300 , as long as about 20 amps covers what you run. Whichever one you pick, switch the converter off once the house batteries are full, and leave the air conditioner to the pedestal.

 A TT-30 connector does not prove 30 A output
 This answer filters for the presence of a TT-30 receptacle; it does not by itself establish the socket's current limit. The C2000 Gen 2 manual caps its TT-30 at 20 A / 2,400 W. Anker's F3800 Plus technical brief gives 3,000 W for its distinct 120 V TT-30 route. Read the exact manual before assuming any of these can supply the RV's full nameplate current.
 Check the RV's full load and the station's shared AC ceiling
 A port limit and the station's total rated output are separate checks. The C2000 Gen 2 shares 2,400 W across its five household outlets and TT-30, so using multiple outlets does not add capacity. The F3800 Plus's 240 V L14-30 route is a separate plan and is not the same as its 120 V TT-30 socket. Compare the RV's voltage, running draw, compressor or air-conditioner startup and simultaneous loads with the exact port and station ratings.
 Match the package and connection, not only the plug
 Confirm the station model, selected package, cord and RV input requirements before connecting. A TT-30 receptacle is not a 240 V output, and an adapter cannot increase a station's documented voltage or watt limit. If your RV requires a full 30 A circuit, treat that as a separate electrical requirement and obtain explicit manufacturer confirmation for the exact station port and operating mode.
 Questions that change the choice
 Does TT-30 mean the station can supply 30 A?
 No. It identifies a connector type, not automatically the station's current limit. The C2000 Gen 2 example is explicitly capped at 20 A; the F3800 Plus TT-30 route is published at up to 3,000 W; the HomePower 3600 Plus port-specific cap is not established in the reviewed record.
 Can I use the station's total AC rating as the TT-30 rating?
 Not unless the manual says that the port can deliver that amount. Overall AC output can be shared among outlets, and a station may impose a lower limit on a specific receptacle.
 Is the F3800 Plus 240 V outlet another TT-30 socket?
 No. The reviewed plan distinguishes a 120 V TT-30 route from a separate 120/240 V L14-30 route. Confirm the exact receptacle and voltage for the load instead of treating the two connector names as interchangeable.

 Short answer: One that we stock: the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus has a native NEMA TT-30 outlet, so a 30 amp shore cord plugs straight into the station. On most other listings TT-30 means the opposite, an input cable that charges the station from a pedestal. Before you buy, check whether the spec sheet names the output receptacle or only a wattage.
 This question gets answered badly all over the internet because the same connector appears on both ends of the product line. Separate the two before you spend anything.
 The stations that actually have one
 The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus carries a NEMA TT-30 receptacle on the unit. Your rig's shore cord goes straight in and the whole coach comes alive: converter, outlets, lights, fridge on electric. Its listing states 3,584Wh of capacity with 3,600W continuous output and 7,200W surge, which matters because a 30 amp RV service is 120V single phase and therefore about 3,600W at the pedestal. It is one of the few stations rated to actually fill that service rather than imitate it.
 It is not the only one on our shelves with the socket. BLUETTI's spec sheets list a 120V/30A NEMA TT-30 outlet on the AC200P L (2,400W in total) and a NEMA TT-30R plus a NEMA 14-50R on the Apex 300 (3,840W in total). The AC200P L's 2,400W is short of the roughly 3,600W a 30 amp pedestal supplies, and the Apex 300's 3,840W is shared across all of its outlets, but on either one a shore cord plugs straight in.
 Be realistic about runtime. 3,584Wh against a rooftop air conditioner pulling roughly 1,500W is about two hours. Against a fridge, lights, water pump and device charging it is a night and most of the next day. The listing states it expands to 21kWh with additional battery packs if that is not enough.
 Two Anker SOLIX stations we now carry also list a TT-30R receptacle: the C2000 Gen 2 (20A, 2,400 W) and the F3800 Plus (25A, up to 3,000 W). Both sit below the 3,600 W a 30-amp service allows. See running a 30-amp RV on an Anker SOLIX .
 Pecron makes two more. The Pecron E3600LFP has a TT-30R outlet and a 3,600W rating on 3,072Wh, and the F3000LFP has a 30A AC outlet on the same 3,072Wh. See Pecron E3600LFP vs F3000LFP .
 TT-30 in, TT-30 out
 A TT-30 input cable plugs a station into a campground pedestal so it charges fast. That is what our BLUETTI TT-30 listings are. The NEMA TT-30 fast charging cable is 60 inches long, fits the AC240 and AC240P, and Bluetti rates maximum input at 2,200W and 2,300W respectively, rising to 2,400W with an expansion battery attached.
 A TT-30 output is the 30 amp receptacle described above. The distinction is the whole question, and most product pages do not spell it out.
 If you have a 50 amp coach instead
 Different socket entirely. The Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus listing states NEMA 14-50 and L14-30R outputs with 7,200W continuous and 120V/240V operation. The 14-50 is the 50 amp RV socket. It does not have a TT-30, so a 30 amp trailer needs an adapter with that unit.
 What to check on any station before you buy
 Does the spec sheet name the output receptacle types , or only a wattage? If it only says watts, assume standard household outlets.
 What is the continuous AC rating? A 1,800W station cannot pretend to be a pedestal no matter which plug is fitted to it.
 Is there a high-current 12V output ? That path skips the inverter entirely for fridge, pump and lighting loads.
 The fixed-install route
 If you would rather feed the coach panel than the shore inlet, there are two paths. A manual transfer switch, such as the Jackery 120V 30A unit with its L5-30 inlet, is pre-wired and removes the back-feeding danger of improvised cords. Or replace the panel: the BLUETTI RV5 is a 5-in-1 hub rated to 5,000W at 120V, and the Epanel takes over from the conventional RV breaker panel with monitored circuits.

Which Power Station Runs a 30 Amp RV? Honest Answer 
 Skip to content

 · ★ 4.7 from 14,397 product reviews 
 Short answer: BLUETTI does make stations with a TT-30 output , and we sell two of them. BLUETTI's own spec sheets list a 120V/30A NEMA TT-30 outlet on the AC200P L (2,400W in total) and a NEMA TT-30R plus a NEMA 14-50R on the Apex 300 (3,840W in total). No EcoFlow station in EcoFlow's own product feed lists one. Anker's spec tables list a TT-30R receptacle on the SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (120V, 20A, 2,400W) and the F3800 Plus (120V, 25A, up to 3,000W), and we now sell both. Whichever box you plug into, the socket is limited by what that station allows (2,400W on the AC200P L and the C2000 Gen 2, 3,000W on the F3800 Plus's TT-30R, 3,840W shared across all Apex 300 outlets), not by the 30 amp rating. Everything else is either an adapter-plus-load-management job or a fixed 48V install that feeds the coach panel.
 What a 30 amp rig is actually asking for
 A 30 amp RV cord ends in a TT-30 plug: one 120-volt leg, thirty amps, a neutral and a ground. Thirty amps at 120 volts is about 3,600 watts, and that is the ceiling the pedestal breaker enforces, not a number your coach draws continuously. What decides whether a power station can run your rig is almost never the plug. It is whether the inverter can start and hold the rooftop air conditioner while the converter, the fridge and the water heater are also awake.
 If what you need is a station that takes over when the pedestal drops, see BLUETTI as backup power: UPS times and RV use .
 Sizing it for your own rig? Answer a few questions about how you camp and our RV solar & battery calculator sizes the bank, array, inverter and controller for you.
 So the question splits in two:
 Connector: is there a physical 30 amp RV receptacle on the box, so the shore cord goes in without an adapter?
 Capacity: can the unit deliver the surge and the sustained watts your coach actually pulls?
 Plenty of stations answer the second. Very few answer the first.
 The input-versus-output confusion that makes most pages wrong
 This is the whole reason we wrote the page. Search "power station with 30 amp RV plug" and you get TT-30 cables presented as TT-30 outlets . They are opposite ends of the system:
 A TT-30 input cable runs from a campground pedestal into the station so the pedestal charges the station. Power flows toward the battery.
 A TT-30 output receptacle is a socket on the station that your coach's shore cord plugs into. Power flows toward the RV.
 Both get written up as "TT-30 compatible". If a listing does not use the words output, outlet or receptacle, assume it is an input. We cover the same distinction on our native TT-30 RV plug answer page .
 What BLUETTI's listings state
 We sell BLUETTI, so we can be specific. Two stations we carry list a TT-30 output on BLUETTI's own spec sheets: the AC200P L , with a 120V/30A NEMA TT-30 outlet beside four 120V/20A outlets (2,400W in total), and the Apex 300 , with a NEMA TT-30R and a NEMA 14-50R (120/240V, 50A) beside four 20A outlets (3,840W in total). BLUETTI's Elite 300 sheet lists a TT-30 port as well. The other TT-30 items in the range are input charging accessories, such as the NEMA TT-30 fast charging cable for the AC240 and AC240P, rated 2,200W and 2,300W maximum input, and the 30A AC300/AC500 charging cable at 3,000W maximum input. Those are pedestal-to-station cables: they charge the unit from a campsite, they do not turn it into one.
 A socket is a connector, not extra power. The TT-30 on an AC200P L still delivers at most the station's 2,400W, and the Apex 300's outlets share its 3,840W, so check your air conditioner's start-up surge before you rely on either. Browse our BLUETTI range .
 What Anker states — in Anker's words
 Anker's SOLIX listings also put TT-30 on the station. Read the wording carefully, because we are quoting it rather than interpreting it. Anker's listing for the SOLIX F3800 Plus says: "EV & RV Charging: Direct charging via NEMA TT-30P or L14-30 ports." The listing for the F3800 Plus + Smart Home Power Kit says: "EV/RV Charging: Direct charging via NEMA TT-30P or L14-30 ports." The non-Plus F3800 and the F3800 + Expansion Battery both say: "EV/RV Charging: Direct charging via NEMA 14-50 or L14-30 ports." 
 Here is why the wording mattered. TT-30 P is the designation for the male plug; a socket built into a power station would normally be called a TT-30 R receptacle, and when we first wrote this page Anker's listings did not settle which one they meant. Update, October 2026: Anker's current F3800 Plus spec table and FAQ list a TT-30R receptacle (120V, 25A, up to 3,000W), and the C2000 Gen 2 spec table lists a TT-30R at 120V, 20A and 2,400W. Both are receptacles a 30 amp shore cord plugs into. One catch on the F3800 Plus: while it is itself plugged into a 120V outlet, Anker says the TT-30R passes power through at up to 1,440W and the L14-30R is off, so unplug it from the wall to get the full 3,000W on the TT-30R.
 We now carry both the C2000 Gen 2 and the F3800 Plus , and they ship from our warehouse in Upland, California. As with BLUETTI, the socket is a connector, not extra power: Anker publishes no surge figure for the F3800 Plus's TT-30R, so check your air conditioner's start-up surge before you rely on it. See running a 30-amp RV on an Anker SOLIX .
 What EcoFlow's feed shows
 No station in EcoFlow's product feed states a native TT-30 output. Where 30 amp connectors appear, they are L14-30 — a 120/240V four-wire generator connector, not an RV shore connector — and they show up on accessories rather than on the stations. EcoFlow's listing for the Double Voltage Hub says: "It also has a NEMA L14-30 outlet, making it that much easier to switch out your old gas generator." Their Home Backup Kit transfer switch listing describes "The NEMA L14-30R to L14-30P generator cord" . Useful for a house backup tie-in, but not a TT-30 socket for your coach.
 Pecron, which we also sell, lists a TT-30R outlet and a 3,600W rating on the E3600LFP and a 30A AC outlet on the F3000LFP , both 3,072Wh. Our E3600LFP vs F3000LFP comparison covers what each can run.

 Route one: adapt from the AC outlets and manage the load
 This is what most people actually do, and it works if you are honest about the load. You take a 30 amp shore-cord adapter from a standard 120V outlet on the station to the TT-30 plug, and you accept that the station's own inverter rating — not the 30 amp connector — is your real limit. A dogbone adapter creates no watts.
 In practice: run the fridge, the lights, the water pump, the converter and the entertainment gear, and stage the heavy items. Air conditioning is the decider, and if the unit cannot start your rooftop unit, no adapter changes that. Check the continuous and surge rating against the compressor's demand, and do not assume a 30 amp shore connection implies 3,600W behind it. Size on watts, not on plugs; our BLUETTI range is here.
 Route two: stop using a plug and feed the coach panel
 The second route is the one nobody searching this question expects, and it is what we would build for a rig that boondocks regularly. Instead of plugging the coach into a box, you replace the coach's electrical spine. The BLUETTI RV5 Modular RV Power System Inverter is a 5-in-1 hub at $1,172.34 that takes the place of the converter, the inverter, the transfer switch, the solar controller and the DC-DC charger, with up to 5,000W at 120V on a 48V system. The BLUETTI Epanel Smart Distribution Panel at $450.34 replaces the conventional breaker panel with smart, monitored circuits, so the house circuits are fed from the system directly. No TT-30 plug is involved, because the shore cord is no longer the path power takes.
 Round it out with the B4810 48V battery at $1,498.00 for 5,120Wh — stackable, with CAN closed-loop communication so the hub manages the pack rather than estimating it — the Epad 10.1-inch control screen at $360.09, and PV100 FX flexible roof panels at $298.99 for a 200W pair. Bought as a package, the 5kWh RV kit is $3,338.34 and the 10kWh kit is $5,402.60. On our own store the 5kWh kit runs $142.43 under the four parts bought singly, while at 10kWh the parts add up to $423.83 less than the kit — we did that arithmetic in full in our kit versus separate parts breakdown , and we would rather you buy the side that suits you. If you are still deciding between 48V and a conventional 12V bank, our 48V versus 12V answer page covers the trade.
 The honest cost of this route is labor and commitment: it is a wiring job inside the coach and it is not portable. Route one is a purchase; route two is an install.

If the goal is a weekend with the fridge cold and the lights on, a station plus a dogbone adapter is the sensible answer and you should size it on watts and surge, not on the shape of the socket. If the goal is a 30 amp receptacle on the side of a box, BLUETTI's AC200P L and Apex 300 both list one, as do Anker's C2000 Gen 2 and F3800 Plus, and the limit is still the station: 2,400W or 3,840W on the BLUETTIs, 2,400W or 3,000W on the Ankers' TT-30R. And if the goal is living in the rig off grid, stop shopping for a plug and build the system: the RV5 and Epanel feed the coach panel, and that setup stops feeling like a workaround after the first month.  How to Size a Portable Power Station for Your RV
 Sizing a power station is less about your RV’s length and more about the sum of what draws electricity while you are away from a hookup. Start by listing your always-on loads rather than your peak loads. A 12V compressor fridge, a router, a CPAP, and a few lights usually total far less than people expect once you measure them.
 The calculation itself is simple. Divide your battery’s watt-hour capacity by 90 percent to account for conversion losses and the charge you should never drain into, then divide that usable figure by the wattage your loads actually draw. For a 2048Wh station that gives roughly 1840Wh usable, and a 45W average fridge load means about 40 hours before the battery is genuinely empty.
 Nameplate numbers mislead here. A compressor fridge rated at 50W but running at 45 percent duty cycle draws closer to 22W on average, and a microwave rated at 1500W only draws that for the minute it runs. Our camping power station guide covers duty cycle math in more detail.
 Continuous output versus startup surge
 This is the number one reason RV owners feel short-changed. A 1500W air conditioner can draw 3000W or more for a moment as the compressor starts, and an inverter that cannot deliver that surge will trip or refuse to start the unit. Always check the surge rating, not just the continuous rating.
 A soft start device on the air conditioner compressor reduces that startup spike, and RVer reports indicate it can let a 2000W inverter start a 1500W AC unit. That single accessory can be the difference between a station being usable for your rig and being decoration. If a CPAP is part of your setup, our CPAP power station picks cover the UPS requirements in more depth.
 Connecting to the RV: TT-30 versus a dogbone adapter
 A TT-30 outlet on the station is the cleanest connection, and only two stations in this roundup have one natively. Everything else needs a 30A to 120V dogbone adapter, which is a perfectly normal RV part, but it adds a failure point and depends on a secure fit in a compartment that gets hot in summer.
 Wire it through a proper RV shore power arrangement with a transfer switch rather than backfeeding the trailer directly. If you want to power trailer electronics rather than the trailer, the 12V/30A DC output on the AC200PL and Elite 300 is the feature to look for.
 Solar input sizing and real-world yield
 Match solar input to the station’s ceiling, not to your ambition. A station with 1200W of solar input, such as the AC200PL or the Elite 300, can absorb a full 400W roof panel array without wasting capability, while units capped at 400W or 600W will ignore the extra panels entirely.
 Expect a real-world yield well below the panel rating. Forum measurements put a 200W panel at closer to 700Wh over a full day rather than the 1000Wh a spec sheet implies, because of heat, angle, shade, and reflection losses. For our budget station roundup picks, budget for panels that are larger than the station’s input rating.
 Cold weather and battery behaviour
 Most units block charging below freezing because charging a lithium cell cold causes metallic lithium plating, which permanently reduces capacity. Warm the station to room temperature before charging in winter conditions, and expect less usable capacity in the cold even when charging is possible. LiFePO4 chemistry holds 85 to 90 percent of rated capacity at minus 12F, compared with 60 to 70 percent for typical lithium-ion.
 Charging from the alternator while you drive
 A DC-to-DC charger is what turns driving hours into battery hours, and a properly sized unit moves several times more power than plugging into the 12V car port. Check your alternator rating and your wire gauge before you start, because an undersized cable on a high-current DC-DC charger gets hot. Our full power station index covers the chargers that pair well with these batteries.
 Power station versus generator
 The honest comparison is not one or the other. A power station is silent, fume-free, and allowed in campsites with strict generator hours, which makes it right for overnight loads. A generator still wins on sustained high-draw appliances and refilling a large battery bank quickly. The most practical setups use both, with the station covering the night and the generator handling the daytime cooking and cooling.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a portable power station run an RV air conditioner?
 Partly. Most RV air conditioners need 1500W to run and can pull 3000W or more at startup, so you need a station with at least 2000W continuous output and surge headroom above that. The DJI Power 2000 at 3000W continuous and the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 with 4000W peak are the strongest options here. Expect roughly 60 to 90 minutes of runtime from a 2048Wh battery, not an entire night. A soft start device on the compressor reduces the startup spike and lets a smaller inverter handle the load.
 Which portable power station has a TT-30 RV plug?
 Only two of the stations in this roundup include a native 30A TT-30 outlet: the BLUETTI AC200PL and the BLUETTI Elite 300. Every other model needs a 30A to 120V dogbone adapter, which is a standard RV part but adds a connection point inside a hot storage compartment. The Elite 300 also adds 12V/30A DC output and 20A AC outlets, which no other unit here combines.
 Can you plug an RV into a portable power station?
 You can power an RV’s appliances through a TT-30 connection, but you should never backfeed a trailer’s shore power inlet directly from a battery. Wire the station through a proper RV transfer or shore power arrangement so the trailer’s built-in protection still applies. Most stations without a TT-30 outlet are used for individual appliances through standard AC plugs instead.
 How long will a 2000Wh power station run a 12V RV fridge?
 A 12V compressor fridge rated around 45W to 55W typically runs at a 40 to 50 percent duty cycle, so its real average draw is close to 20W to 27W. From a 2048Wh battery with about 90 percent usable capacity, that works out to roughly 60 to 80 hours of continuous operation before charging. In practice you will be topping up from solar well before that point.
 Are portable power stations better than a generator for RV camping?
 They are better for overnight and low-draw use. A power station is silent, produces no exhaust, works inside the trailer, and complies with campground quiet hours that often ban generators after a set time. Generators remain better for sustained high-draw appliances such as a microwave, electric heat, or an air conditioner running for hours. Most full-time RVers run a station for the evening and a generator for daytime cooking.
 The Portable Power Station I Would Buy for an RV in 2026
 After putting all ten through the same routine, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 remains the pick we would hand to most RV owners. It is light enough to reposition alone, the app is clear, and the 1500W output covers everything a typical weekend of fridge, CPAP, and evening use demands.
 For longer boondocking trips, the BLUETTI AC200PL is the stronger machine, with a native TT-30 port and expandability to 8448Wh. Smaller trailers and couples should look at the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 for value, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 for fast UPS behaviour with medical devices, and the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 if you plan to charge from the alternator. Full-time installers running heavier loads belong with the BLUETTI Elite 300 or the DJI Power 2000.
 Whichever route you take for the best portable power stations for RV camping , measure your actual loads before buying, check the surge rating against your air conditioner, and confirm the connection type your rig needs. Those three checks prevent nearly every regret we heard about from owners.

 What Should You Check Before Buying?
 Don’t choose a 30A RV power station based on the TT-30 outlet alone.
 Check these four things first.
 1. The RV outlet 
 If you want to connect an RV 30A shore-power cord, look for a NEMA TT-30 or TT-30R connection.
 Also check whether the manufacturer requires a grounding adapter. The Jackery HomePower 3000 is a good example: it has a TT-30 port, but Jackery says an adapter is required for direct RV use.
 2. Continuous output 
 This determines how much power the station can provide while your appliances are running.
 A 30A RV connection does not automatically mean the power station can continuously provide 3,600W.
 Always check the manufacturer’s specifications for the actual outlet and inverter.
 3. Battery capacity 
 Battery capacity is measured in watt-hours (Wh) .
 A higher Wh rating means more stored energy and generally allows longer runtime at the same load.
 If you’re unfamiliar with how these systems store and deliver electricity, see our guide on how a portable power station works .
 For example, the DELTA Pro 3 starts with 4,096Wh, while the Elite 300 has 3,014.4Wh.
 4. Startup power 
 Some RV appliances use considerably more power when starting than they do while running.
 Air conditioners, refrigerators, pumps, and other motor-driven equipment can have startup demands that affect whether a power station can operate them.
 Check the appliance and power station specifications rather than relying on a generic startup multiplier.
 Can a 30A RV Power Station Run an RV Air Conditioner?
 Some can, but it depends on the specific air conditioner and power station. 
 An RV air conditioner can be one of the largest loads in the RV. The power station needs enough continuous output to handle the running load and enough starting capability for the compressor.
 A 2,400W station such as the Elite 300 may work with some RV AC setups, but you should check the specific air conditioner’s requirements first.
 Higher-output options such as the Apex 300 and DELTA Pro 3 provide substantially more power headroom.
 Battery capacity matters too. A power station can have enough output to run an air conditioner but still provide only limited runtime before the battery needs recharging.
 How Long Will a 30A RV Power Station Last?
 There is no single runtime figure for a 30A RV connection.
 Your actual runtime depends on the average power draw of the RV , not simply the size of the plug.
 A basic estimate is:
 Runtime ≈ usable battery capacity ÷ average power draw 
 For example, a power station with 3,000Wh of usable energy running a 500W average load would have a theoretical runtime of about 6 hours before accounting for conversion losses and other factors.
 Actual runtime can be shorter because of inverter losses, battery-management limits, temperature, battery condition, and changes in appliance power consumption.
 If you plan to boondock for several days, solar charging and expandable battery capacity can become just as important as the size of the RV outlet.
 For more information on charging options and charging times, see our guide on how to charge a portable power station .
 Native TT-30 vs. Adapter: Which Is Better?
 If your RV uses a standard 30A shore-power connection, a native TT-30/TT-30R outlet is generally the simpler option .
 You can use the compatible RV connection without adding an adapter between the power station and the RV.
 However, always follow the manufacturer’s instructions. A TT-30 outlet by itself does not guarantee that the station can directly power an RV without additional grounding equipment.
 And remember:
 An adapter changes the connection. It does not increase the power station’s output. 
 A 1,800W power station does not become a 3,600W power station simply because you connect a 30A adapter.
 Final Verdict
 For most RV owners looking for a portable power station with a 30A connection, the BLUETTI Apex 300 is the best overall choice .
 It combines a 2,764.8Wh battery, 3,840W total AC output, and a dedicated TT-30R outlet rated up to 3,600W . That gives it an excellent balance of RV compatibility and high-power capability.
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the better choice if you want more starting battery capacity, 4,000W of continuous output, and substantial expansion potential.
 The Jackery HomePower 3000 is a strong 3kWh-class alternative with 3,600W of output, but remember that Jackery requires a grounding adapter for RV connection.
 The BLUETTI Elite 300 is the better compact option if you want around 3kWh of capacity and a native TT-30 connection without stepping up to a much larger system.
 If you also need a power station for home outages, see our guide to the best portable power stations for home backup .
 The most important rule: don’t buy based on the 30A label alone. Check the actual TT-30 outlet rating, continuous output, battery capacity, startup requirements, and RV connection requirements before buying.

 Yes, when the specific power station is designed to support direct RV connection through its TT-30/TT-30R outlet . However, some models have additional grounding requirements. For example, Jackery says its HomePower 3000 requires a grounding adapter for RV use.

 Good: lots of energy and output for the weight, full 30 A RV port, 3+2-year warranty.
 Watch out: not expandable. Jackery rates cycle life to 70% (4,000 cycles), not 80%. Jackery says its stations aren’t recommended for medical devices.
 Best for: mid-size trailers that want 3 kWh without a 100-lb box.
 Check the Jackery HomePower 3000 price on Amazon 
 5. Jackery Explorer 2000 v2: lightest 2 kWh station
 At about 39.5 lb, the Explorer 2000 v2 is the lightest 2 kWh LiFePO4 station in our catalog. It holds 2,042 Wh, runs 2,200 W from three AC outlets with a 4,400 W surge, and Jackery rates it at 30 dB in quiet mode. It charges from the wall in 1.75 hours (1.3 hours in Emergency Charge mode) and takes up to 400 W of solar. There’s no RV outlet, so it’s built for running appliances directly with cords rather than powering the whole coach.
 Good: easy to lift in and out, quiet, strong surge for its size.
 Watch out: no TT-30 outlet, not expandable, slow car charging (Jackery lists 24 hours), modest solar input. Cycle life is rated to 70%.
 Best for: pop-ups, truck campers and smaller trailers where you plug in only a few things.
 Check the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 price on Amazon 
 6. EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: best for van life
 In a van, space and charging on the move matter more than raw size. The DELTA 3 Plus is 27.6 lb, holds 1,024 Wh (expandable to 5 kWh with EcoFlow extra batteries) and runs 1,800 W. Its big advantage is charging: up to 1,000 W of solar from roof panels, and with EcoFlow’s 800W Alternator Charger it fills in about 1.3 hours of driving. EcoFlow says it’s 30 dB under 600 W and switches to battery in under 10 ms if you’re plugged in at a campground and the power drops.
 Good: compact, very fast charging from the road and the roof, expandable, 5-year warranty.
 Watch out: no RV outlet, and 1,800 W is too close to a roof AC’s running draw to rely on. The alternator charger costs extra (about $269 at EcoFlow) and EcoFlow recommends professional installation.
 Best for: camper vans with a 12 V fridge, fan, lights and laptops.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus price on Amazon 
 RV power basics: 30 amp, 50 amp and what a station can run
 Your RV’s shore power cord tells you how much it was built to use. A 30-amp RV runs on one 120-volt circuit: 120 V × 30 A = 3,600 W at most. A 50-amp RV has two 120-volt legs of 50 A each, up to 12,000 W in total. No portable station comes close to 50-amp service, and only a few can deliver the full 3,600 W of a 30-amp cord.
 Plugging your shore cord into a station’s TT-30 outlet feeds the whole coach, so everything that normally runs on shore power tries to run from the battery. Before you do, switch off the big loads at the breaker panel: the air conditioner, the electric side of the water heater and the electric mode of an absorption fridge. Your RV’s converter will also start charging the house battery from the station, which uses up energy you may want for other things. A 50-amp RV needs a 50-to-30 adapter to plug into a TT-30 outlet, and then it gets only 30-amp power.
 The RV fridge. Many RVs have an absorption fridge that runs on propane or on a 120 V heating element. Replacement elements for common Dometic and Norcold models are rated about 195 to 325 W. If a 300 W element ran nonstop, it would use 7.2 kWh a day, more than any station here holds. It cycles, so real use is lower, but on battery, leave the fridge on propane. A 12 V compressor fridge is a far better match: Dometic rates its CFX3 45 at 1.03 Ah per hour at 12 V in 90°F heat, about 300 Wh a day, so a 2 kWh station (about 1,740 Wh usable) runs it for roughly five to six days by our estimate.
 The roof air conditioner, honestly. Dometic lists 1,731 W in cooling mode for its Penguin II 13.5K roof unit, and EcoFlow’s RV guide uses about 1,500 W running and about 2,800 W to start for a typical 13,500 BTU unit. That start-up surge rules out most stations under 2,000 W. And even when a station can start it, the math is short: 4,096 Wh × 0.85 ÷ 1,731 W ≈ 2 hours of nonstop cooling; a 2 kWh station gives about 1 hour. A soft starter, which EcoFlow says can cut the start-up surge by 50 to 65%, helps a station start the AC but doesn’t make the battery last longer. For all-day cooling, you still need shore power, a generator where allowed, or a very large battery and solar system.
 How to choose a portable power station for an RV
 Do the math: list what you’ll run, multiply watts × hours for a daily total, and compare it with usable energy (capacity × 0.85). Example: a 12 V compressor fridge uses about 300 Wh a day in hot weather; add your lights, fans, water pump, laptops and phones from their labels, plus a microwave at its label watts × the hours you use it. A 2 kWh station gives about 1,740 Wh usable, which is why it suits a weekend of dry camping.
 Look for a TT-30 outlet: if you want to plug the whole coach in, you need it. Check its amp rating: the Jackery HomePower 3000 rates its port at 30 A, the Anker C2000 Gen 2 at 20 A.
 Charge while driving: a 12 V socket gives about 100 W (EcoFlow’s figure), too slow for a 2 kWh battery. Alternator chargers (EcoFlow 800 W, Anker 800 W, BLUETTI 560 W) are wired to the vehicle battery; have a pro install them.
 Solar input: roof or portable panels are what make multi-day boondocking work. Check each station’s maximum watts and voltage range before buying panels.
 Cold weather: LiFePO4 batteries shouldn’t be charged below freezing. EcoFlow, Jackery and Anker list 32°F as the lowest charging temperature for the models here. In winter, keep the station inside the heated coach.
 Weight and space: anything over about 60 lb needs a fixed home in the RV or wheels. Secure it so it can’t slide when you brake.
 A power station is also the quiet answer to campground generator rules. In national parks, generators can’t exceed 60 decibels at 50 feet (36 CFR 2.12), and parks limit their hours: Grand Canyon’s Mather Campground allows them only 7 to 9 am and 6 to 8 pm. A battery has no engine, so it keeps running through quiet hours. If you do carry a gas generator, the CPSC says to run it outdoors only, at least 20 feet from buildings, with the exhaust pointed away from windows, doors and vents.
 Keep exploring: our portable power stations guide explains sizing in depth. See also the best power stations for camping , the best solar generators , power stations for a refrigerator and power station vs. generator . For the bigger picture, read off-grid energy explained , or browse all portable power station articles .
 RV power station questions
 Can a portable power station run an RV air conditioner?
 Only briefly. A 13,500 BTU roof unit uses about 1,500 to 1,731 W while cooling and needs a start-up surge around 2,800 W. Large stations like the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 can start it, but by our estimate 4,096 Wh lasts about two hours of nonstop cooling and a 2 kWh station about one. Use the AC on shore power, and the station for everything else.
 What size power station do I need for my RV?
 For a weekend of dry camping without the air conditioner, 2,000 Wh suits most travel trailers. Vans with a 12 V fridge and laptops do well with 1,000 Wh plus solar or an alternator charger. Big motorhomes that boondock for days should look at 3,000 to 4,000 Wh and expandable systems. Add up your daily watt-hours and multiply the station’s capacity by 0.85 for losses.
 Can I plug my RV into a portable power station?
 Yes, if the station has a TT-30 outlet, like the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2, BLUETTI AC200L or Jackery HomePower 3000. Turn off the AC, the electric water heater and the fridge’s electric mode first. Check the outlet’s amp rating and the maker’s instructions; Jackery, for example, says the HomePower 3000 needs a grounding adapter to power an RV.
 Can I charge a power station while driving my RV or van?
 Yes. The 12 V socket gives about 100 W, which is slow for big stations: Anker lists 23 hours for the C2000 Gen 2. An alternator charger is much faster. EcoFlow’s 800 W model fills a DELTA 3 Plus in about 1.3 hours, and Anker lists 100% in 3 hours for the C2000 Gen 2. These are wired to the vehicle battery, so have them installed properly.
 Will a power station run my RV refrigerator?
 A 12 V compressor fridge, easily: Dometic’s CFX3 45 uses about 300 Wh a day in hot weather, so a 1 kWh station lasts nearly three days by our estimate. An absorption fridge on electric is a poor match, because its 120 V heating element draws roughly 195 to 325 W while on. Run an absorption fridge on propane when you’re off shore power.
 Is a portable power station better than a generator for an RV?
 For quiet, everyday loads, yes: no fuel, no fumes and no generator-hour limits. For running a roof AC all afternoon, a generator or shore power still wins. Many RVers carry both and use the generator, during allowed hours and well away from the coach, to recharge the station. Our power station vs. generator guide compares them.

 Best Portable Power Stations for RVs (2026): Shore Power in a Box
 By Daniel Foster Updated October 15, 2026 RV 
When you buy through our links, we may earn a commission at no cost to you.
 It never changes our picks. How we work 
 An RV already has a power system — shore power at 30 or 50 amps. A portable power station doesn’t replace that; it replaces the generator : silent power for boondocking, overnighting at a Walmart, or keeping the fridge and furnace blower alive when the campground pedestal fails. Sizing one honestly means talking about the air conditioner first.
 How we picked: verified manufacturer specs (including outlet types, which marketing pages often bury), RV-owner community reports, and runtime math below. We have not bench-tested every unit; where hands-on matters, we say so. How we work .
 The short version
 Pick Unit Capacity AC output Why it wins 
 Best overall Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 2,048Wh 2,400W, TT-30 RV outlet A real 30A RV port — still rare in this class 
 Best budget Bluetti AC180 1,152Wh 1,800W Cheapest LiFePO4 unit worth dogboning into a rig 
 Best for solar boondocking Bluetti AC200L 2,048Wh 2,400W 1,200W solar input — the highest here 
 Best for 50A rigs Anker Solix F3800 3,840Wh 6,000W, 240V, 14-50 outlet 240V split-phase; feeds a 50A panel properly 
 Best simple Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus 2,042Wh 3,000W Wheels, no-fuss UI, huge expansion ceiling 
 RV power in 60 seconds
 30-amp service = 120V × 30A = 3,600W maximum. Most travel trailers.
 50-amp service = 240V split-phase = 12,000W maximum. Big fifth wheels and motorhomes.
 What that service feeds:
 RV load Typical draw Notes 
 Roof AC (13.5k BTU) 1,300–1,600W running Startup surge 2,800–3,500W; a soft-start kit cuts that roughly in half 
 Microwave 1,000–1,500W Short bursts — fine on any 2kW unit 
 Converter (charging house batteries) 300–600W Flip its breaker off when running from a power station — see below 
 Electric water heater element ~1,400W Run it on propane instead 
 RV fridge on AC 150–300W cycling Run it on propane instead; it sips 12V/propane 
 Furnace blower, fans, lights, water pump 50–150W total These run off 12V DC — your house battery, not the station 
 The pattern: the big loads all have propane or 12V alternatives. A power station’s real job is outlets, TV, coffee maker, device charging, and the occasional microwave — which is why 2kWh covers a boondocking weekend comfortably.
 Three ways to hook it up
 1. Plug devices straight into the station. Simplest, nothing to configure. Run an extension cord through a window for the coffee maker and TV.
 2. Dogbone the shore cord into the station. A 15A-to-TT-30 adapter lets you plug the whole rig in — every outlet in the RV goes live. Three rules: switch the fridge and water heater to gas, flip the converter breaker off (otherwise the station spends 300–600W charging your house batteries — a pointless loop), and remember you’re capped around 1,800W unless the station has a native TT-30.
 3. Native TT-30 or 14-50. The Anker C2000 Gen 2’s TT-30 outlet and the F3800’s 14-50 outlet feed the rig at full output. This is the clean setup for regular boondockers.
 The EMS gotcha: if your rig has a progressive EMS/surge protector, it may refuse power station output with an open-ground or open-neutral error. That’s the floating neutral — the standard fix is a neutral-ground bonding plug (a few dollars) in a spare outlet on the station.
 The air conditioner reality check
 Yes, a 2,400W+ station can start and run a 13.5k BTU roof AC — especially with a soft-start kit taming the surge. No, you cannot run it all afternoon: 1,500W × hours = the entire 2kWh battery in about 80 minutes. The realistic use is 30–60 minutes of cooling to knock the heat down, or overnight duty paired with 800W+ of solar the next day. If AC is the mission, buy the biggest expandable system you can — or accept that generators still win this one.
 Our picks, in detail
 Best overall: Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2
 2,048Wh, 2,400W output (4,000W peak), and a built-in TT-30 RV outlet at 41.7 lbs — light enough that one person can actually lift it into a storage bay, no wheels required. It recharges to 100% in under an hour on wall power (58 minutes by Anker’s own spec) and accepts Anker’s BP2000 expansion battery for roughly 4kWh. For most travel-trailer owners this is the box: plug the shore cord straight in, flip the converter breaker off, done. (It replaces the older F2000 — same capacity and RV port, about 25 lbs lighter.)
 → Check price on Amazon 
 Best budget: Bluetti AC180
 1,152Wh and 1,800W for hundreds less than the big units. It’ll run everything except the AC (it can start some soft-started units, but runtime is short), and it dogbones into the shore cord fine within its 1,800W ceiling. Buy it for weekend boondocking on a budget, not for desert summers.
 → Check price on Amazon 
 Best for solar boondocking: Bluetti AC200L
 The AC200L’s 1,200W max solar input is the number that matters off-grid: it can actually swallow a rooftop array’s output, refilling its 2,048Wh in under two hours of good sun. 2,400W output covers everything but sustained AC duty, and it expands with Bluetti’s B-series batteries. It’s ~62 lbs — set it in a bay and leave it.
 → Check price on Amazon 
 Best for 50A rigs: Anker Solix F3800
 3,840Wh, 6,000W, 240V split-phase with a NEMA 14-50 outlet — the same connector your 50A shore cord uses. It feeds both legs of a 50A panel properly and expands to 26.9kWh for coach owners who want generator-class capability without the generator. At 132 lbs it lives in a bay, not a hatch. See our home backup guide for its dual-use case.
 → Check price on Amazon 
 Best simple: Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus
 No RV outlet, no 240V — just 2,042Wh, a 3,000W inverter, wheels, and the friendliest interface in the category, expandable all the way to 24kWh later. If the person using it doesn’t want to think about breakers and bonding plugs, this is the one. Pair it with a dogbone and the converter-breaker rule. And take the air-conditioner section above to heart: Jackery’s own community has a classic post from an owner who tried to run a mobile-boutique AC off a 2000 Plus and drained it in one hour — 3,000W of inverter clears the surge easily, but 2kWh is 30–60 minutes of cooling, not an afternoon.
 → Check price on Amazon 
 Related reading: overlanding power (fridge-first builds and alternator charging), and the brand-by-brand breakdown .
 FAQ
 (Quick answers at the top of this page. Rig-specific question? Ask us .) 
 Frequently asked questions
 Can a portable power station run an RV air conditioner? Technically yes on larger units: a 13,500 BTU RV air conditioner draws roughly 1,300–1,600W running with a startup surge around 2,800–3,500W, so you need at least a 2,400W-class inverter. The catch is runtime — at ~1,500Wh per hour, a 2,048Wh battery buys about an hour of cooling. Plan on short stints, or add a soft-start kit and serious solar.
 Can I plug my RV's 30-amp cord into a power station? Yes, two ways. Some units (like the Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2) have a native TT-30 RV outlet. Everything else works through a 15A-to-TT-30 'dogbone' adapter on a standard outlet — but then you're limited to roughly 1,800W, so run the water heater and fridge on propane and watch the air conditioner.
 Why does my EMS or surge protector reject power from a power station? Most power stations output a floating neutral, which progressive EMS units flag as an open ground/neutral fault. The standard fix is a neutral-ground bonding plug in one of the station's other outlets — a $10 part that RV communities have used on inverter generators for years.
 What size power station do I need for RV boondocking? Weekenders running lights, fans, devices and a water pump: 1–2kWh plus a 200–400W panel. Full-timers: a 2kWh expandable base unit, 400W+ of solar, and an alternator or DC-DC charger for driving days. Air conditioning changes everything — see the runtime math below.

results.text:
BLUETTI's Elite 300 Puts An RV Outlet On A 3kWh Power Station Skip to content 
 Photo from bluettipower.com 
 Say you have a 30 amp trailer and want to run it off a battery for a weekend, with no inverter install and no generator. Bluetti’s Elite 300 is built for that: 3,014 watt-hours in a box about 14 inches long and a foot wide and tall, with a TT-30 outlet on the front. Your shore power cord plugs straight into it, like a campground pedestal. No adapters, no rewiring.
 We haven’t tested one ourselves, so everything below comes from Bluetti’s manual and spec sheet, plus our own math. The Elite 300 is sold on Bluetti’s site , and it’s also on Amazon. Looking for panels? Jump to the solar section .
 Photo: bluettipower.com 
 Bluetti Elite 300
 A 3 kWh power station with a TT-30 RV outlet in a compact box, for 30 amp rigs that want quiet power for the fridge, lights, laptops and coffee.
 3,014 Wh Capacity
 2,400 W AC output
 1,200 W Solar input
 Check price at Bluetti 
 Also available at Amazon 
 Buy it if you
 Have a 30 amp (TT-30) RV plug
 Want 3 kWh in a small box
 Plan to charge from solar panels
 Like checking power from your phone
 Skip it if you
 Need the AC running all night
 Charge outside below freezing
 Can’t lift 58 pounds alone
 Want to add batteries later
 A lot of power for a small box
 Key features
 Capacity: 3,014.4Wh (LiFePO4)
 AC output: 2,400W continuous, 120V
 Outlets: 1 TT-30 RV outlet, 4 standard 120V outlets
 DC outputs: 12V/30A port, 12V/10A car socket, USB-C 140W and 100W, 2 USB-A
 Solar input: XT60, 12V to 60V, 22A, 1,200W max
 Wall charging: up to 1,800W
 Wall plus solar: up to 2,400W
 Backup switchover: 10 ms
 App: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
 Size: 14.41 x 12.01 x 11.71 in
 Weight: about 58 lbs
 The Elite 300 stores 3,014 watt-hours in 14.41 by 12.01 by 11.71 inches, about 1.2 cubic feet. A watt-hour is one watt used for one hour, so 3,014 of them would run a 100 watt load for about 30 hours. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is 1,000 of them, which is why it’s called a 3 kWh station.
 Bluetti says it’s the smallest power station by volume in the 3 kWh class, as of January 2026 (a claim certified by Frost & Sullivan, as Electrek reported in March 2026). That’s a lot of battery for something that fits on the floor of a pickup cab or in a pass-through bay.
 To put it in RV terms: a 12 volt, 100Ah lithium battery holds about 1,280 watt-hours. The Elite 300 holds more than two of those, and the inverter, the solar charge controller and the wall charger are already inside the case. The battery is LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate), the same chemistry as most RV lithium batteries.
 The catch is weight. At about 58 pounds, it’s in the range Bluetti’s own manual calls a two-person lift (39.7 to 70.5 pounds). Plan where it lives in the rig before it arrives.
 What the TT-30 outlet does, and what it can’t
 TT-30 is the three-prong, 30 amp, 120 volt plug on most travel trailers and smaller motorhomes, the one that goes into the 30 amp socket on a campground pedestal. On the Elite 300 it’s the round outlet at the top right, above the four standard outlets. Plug your shore power cord in, flip on AC, and the rig runs on the battery, within the limit below.
 The limit is the inverter, the part that turns the battery’s power into the household-style AC power your outlets give. All the AC outlets share 2,400 watts, about 20 amps at 120 volts. A 30 amp pedestal can supply up to 3,600 watts. So the Elite 300 runs a 30 amp rig, but not everything in it at once. A microwave and a coffee maker together will get you close to the limit. If you’re new to amp ratings, our piece on the differences between 30 and 50 amp RVs covers what your rig can draw.
 Two things to know before you plug in:
 Your RV’s converter will start charging your house batteries from the Elite 300 as soon as it sees shore power. That draws watts you may want for other things. If your RV batteries don’t need it, turn off the converter’s breaker.
 A 50 amp rig needs a 50 to 30 amp adapter (a dogbone) to plug in, and it still gets 2,400 watts at most. Our 30 amp cords and adapters guide lists the options.
 Can it run the RV air conditioner?
 Briefly, and only sometimes. A 13,500 BTU rooftop AC pulls somewhere around 1,300 to 1,500 watts running, so, by our math, a full battery buys you roughly two hours of cooling. Starting is the harder part. Bluetti’s manual warns that motors and compressors can pull 2 to 4 times their rated power when they start, which can overload the station. Many rooftop units need a soft start kit (a small add-on that eases the surge when the compressor kicks on) to start on a battery at all.
 The Power Lifting mode won’t help here. It lets the Elite 300 run heating devices rated up to 4,800 watts (kettles, hair dryers, electric blankets), but the manual is clear that the actual output stays at 2,400 watts, so those devices get 2,400 at most. It isn’t for motors or compressors.
 This is a fridge, lights, laptops and coffee battery. Add some solar and, by our math below, it should carry a weekend of everything except the AC.
 What it can run, by our math
 These are our estimates, not Bluetti’s. We assume you lose 10 to 15 percent to the inverter when running AC devices, which is normal for a power station, and less when you use the 12 volt port.
 A 12 volt compressor fridge averaging 45 watts on the 12V/30A port: around 60 hours, two and a half days.
 A residential RV fridge on the TT-30 outlet, using about 1.5 kWh a day: around a day and a half. Check the label on your fridge, because they vary a lot.
 A 1,000 watt coffee maker for 10 minutes: about 170 watt-hours at the pot, closer to 200 with the inverter loss, or 6 to 7 percent of the battery.
 LED lights, a roof fan and phone charging : days. These barely move the battery.
 Charging it: wall, generator, car and solar
 From a wall outlet, the Elite 300 charges at up to 1,800 watts in Turbo mode. Bluetti estimates 80 percent in about 95 minutes. Standard mode (1,200 watts) fills it in about 2.8 hours, and Silent mode in about 4.2 hours for when you’re charging next to the bed.
 Generator: use one with pure sine wave output (clean power like a wall outlet, which inverter generators make). For a generator that surges and dips, the manual says to turn on Grid Self-Adaption mode in the app. Our list of the quietest generators for RV camping has good matches.
 Car: Bluetti’s car cable (sold separately, like the solar cable) plugs into a 12 or 24 volt socket, with the engine running. It’s a top-up while you drive, not a fast charge.
 Solar: up to 1,200 watts, and up to 2,400 watts when solar and wall power charge together. More on panels below.
 Three limits from the manual matter for campers. It only charges between 32 and 104°F, so in winter it charges inside the rig, not in a cold bay (it can run devices down to -4°F). Bluetti rates it for use up to 6,561 feet of altitude, which rules out some of the high camps in the Rockies. And it’s rated IP20, which means no protection from water: keep it out of the rain.
 When the rig sits for the winter, the manual says to store the Elite 300 powered off at 40 to 60 percent, somewhere between 14 and 104°F, and to run it through a full charge and discharge every few months.
 Solar panels for the Elite 300 (XT60 input)
 Solar goes into the XT60 port, the DC/PV input on the front. Bluetti’s limits for it are 12 to 60 volts open circuit voltage (Voc), 22 amps and 1,200 watts. Any brand of panel with MC4 connectors works as long as the panels together stay inside those numbers, and the manual says not to mix different types of panels on one input.
 The MC4 to XT60 cable isn’t in the box with the station, so order one with it. Bluetti’s own is rated 20 amps. Bateria Power sells 12 and 10 AWG adapters in different lengths that can handle higher amperages if needed.
 The rule of thumb: panels in series add their voltages, panels in parallel add their amps. Add up the Voc printed on each panel’s label and keep the total at about 54 volts or less.
 Why Voc and not Vmp? Vmp (the voltage at maximum power) is what panels run at while they charge, and it’s the number for working out watts. But whenever the station stops pulling power, like when the battery is full or before charging starts in the morning, the input sees the full Voc. That’s why Bluetti’s manual puts the 60 volt limit on Voc.
 A panel’s voltage climbs on cold mornings, and Bluetti’s solar panel guide says never to go past the limit, “particularly during cold weather.” Our guides show how to find your panel’s voltage and how to connect two or more panels .
 Panel setups on the Elite 300
 One or two Bluetti PV350 panels: one panel (46.5 volts) plugs straight in. Two have to go in parallel, never in series (93 volts), and together they come to about 21.6 amps, right at the limit, so check the label and the cable.
 Two Bluetti PV200D panels in series: about 49 to 52 volts and 400 watts. Four, as two series pairs in parallel, give 800 watts. Our PV200 review covers what it’s like to set up and fold away.
 Two Renogy 100W rigid panels in series: about 45 volts and 200 watts. Two of those pairs in parallel give 400 watts at under 12 amps.
 Two Renogy 200W rigid panels in series: about 46 volts and 400 watts (check the label: older versions run higher). Stop at two: four come to just over 22 amps.
 The 1,200 watt rating is a ceiling. By our math, a setup that stays inside 60 volts and 22 amps tops out around 1,000 watts. In good sun, 400 watts of panels fill the Elite 300 in about two sunny days, and 800 watts in about 5 hours. Our guides to how long solar charging takes and solar panels for Bluetti power stations go further.
 The app does more than show the battery
 The Elite 300 connects to the Bluetti app over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and the app is where most of the settings live. You can check the battery and see watts coming in and going out from inside the rig, instead of walking out to the bay. From the app you can also:
 Turn the AC and DC outputs on and off, each on its own
 Set charge and discharge limits, so it stops at the percentage you pick
 Pick the wall charging speed (Standard, Turbo or Silent)
 Set the ECO mode thresholds that shut off an output after a period of low or no load. Leave ECO off when a fridge or the lights are plugged in: the manual warns it can switch them off
 Turn on Grid Self-Adaption for an unsteady generator
 Update the firmware, which the manual says to do before first use
 The backup modes are the clever part. Plug the Elite 300 into the pedestal and the RV into the Elite 300, and the rig runs on campground power, with the station switching to battery in 10 milliseconds if the power drops. That’s fast enough that most devices never notice. One limit: in this pass-through setup the station passes only 1,800 watts from the outlet, less than the 2,400 it gives on battery, so it’s a trick for a flaky pedestal, not the way to hook up every night. The app has four modes: Standard (backup when the power fails), Time Control (charge during cheap off-peak hours at home), PV Priority (charge from the wall to a percentage you set, then let solar do the rest) and Custom, where you set the schedule and limits yourself.
 Who should skip it
 If you want the rooftop AC running through a hot night, no 3 kWh station will do that. Bluetti’s page and manual also mention no expansion battery for the Elite 300, so plan on the capacity you buy being the capacity you have.
 If you need more than that, Bluetti’s own summer RV kits move to larger systems: the Apex 300 with expansion batteries for travel trailers and Class Cs, and the RV5 for Class As and full-timers. For smaller and lighter options, our portable power station roundup compares what we’d pick.
 Would you run your rig from a TT-30 power station, or does your setup need more than 2,400 watts? Tell us in the comments.

 Buying Guide: Key Considerations For 30A-Outfitted Portable Power Stations
 Output and surge capacity: Look for a 30A TT-30 RV outlet or equivalent, plus a healthy peak wattage to handle motors, HVAC units, or power tools during startup. Capacity matters for long runs between charges.
 Battery chemistry and longevity: LiFePO4 chemistry offers longer cycle life and better temperature stability, reducing replacement frequency and extending uptime in harsh environments.
 Expandability: If you anticipate growing power needs, choose models with add-on battery options or modular packs to reach higher total capacities without replacing the unit.
 Charging speed and sources: Fast AC charging, solar MPPT support, and even vehicle charging help minimize downtime. Check 0–80% or 0–100% times and the supported solar input wattage.
 Safety features: BMS protections against short circuits, overcharging, and overheating are essential. Look for overcurrent and thermal protections, as well as certifications where available.
 Port variety: A mix of AC outlets, USB-C PD, USB-A, DC, and car ports expands compatibility with laptops, cameras, medical devices, and household appliances.
 Portability vs. capacity: Heavier, higher-capacity units are powerful but less portable. Balance weight, size, and carrying comfort against your travel needs.
 RV compatibility: For RV users, ensure there is a dedicated TT-30 or RV-ready outlet and consider how you’ll manage plugging into campground hookups or solar panels.

 How long a 2kWh power station lasts in an RV
 A 12 V compressor fridge uses about 0.7 kWh a day, a furnace blower 0.3–0.5 kWh on a cold night, and lights, phones and the water pump about 0.2 kWh: roughly 1.2–1.5 kWh a day. That is about a day and a half with no sun, and two to three days with 200–400 W of solar. A 13,500 BTU rooftop AC needs 2,800–3,500 W to start (about 2,000 W with a soft starter) and runs 1,300–1,900 W, so a 2kWh station runs it for about an hour.
 Recharging on the road
 Campground or home outlet: about 1–1.5 hours on a 15/20 A outlet.
 Driving: a DC-DC alternator charger adds 560–800 W; the 12 V socket gives about 100 W, a full day for a full charge.
 Solar: a 400 W panel returns about 1–1.5 kWh on a good day. The AC200L and Renogy take 1,200 W, the Elite 200 V2 1,000 W, Anker 800 W, Jackery 400 W.
 The Elite 200 V2 is lighter and rated for twice the cycles of the AC200L, but has no RV outlet: it needs a 5-20P to TT-30R adapter and is then limited to that outlet's 20 A. Jackery's Explorer 2000 v2 is a popular pick but was $999 on Jackery's store on 2026-10-31 and has no RV outlet.
